title: Anthropic Just Revealed How Their Engineers Use Claude Code
summary: Walks through Felix Rieseberg's essay on being more ambitious with models: ask for outcomes instead of tasks, and push on altitude, depth and range. Give the agent real resources and an outside judge so it can work toward the result rather than the next step.

title: Claude Mods Are Insane... You Need To Try These Right Now
summary: Anthropic's new Claude mods are always-on extensions that can redraw Claude Code's UI and change its behavior, unlike skills or plugins that only add capabilities. The channel builds mods for prompt enhancement, assumption tracking, session dashboards, same-folder session coordination, an idea shelf, and plain-language answer rewriting checked by a Haiku model. The idea worth keeping is the assumptions-review mod: surface every silent assumption the agent made, let a human mark each right or wrong, and automatically feed the wrong ones back as a correction prompt.

title: Google Just Fixed AI Design By Releasing This
summary: Google's Stitch design tool now ships a CLI, so Claude Code can drive it directly without the Google Cloud MCP setup, and it loads into context only when needed. The video builds a workflow of an interview-generated brief.md, Stitch designs, a build from them, then two review skills (design-fidelity and responsive screenshots, then a harsh 'story review' judged against the brief). The idea worth keeping is a written brief as the single source of truth, plus separate review-skill passes that catch what the generating agents miss.

title: GitHub's #1 Trending Skill Is Insane (5 Use Cases)
summary: The video shows 'Reverse Engineer Anything' (REA), an MCP server with ~170 tools that lets Claude Code trace browser behavior down to the exact network requests and code, saving each capture as evidence tagged seen/guessed/unknown. It demos five uses: cloning features from other apps, competitor research, black-box feature testing (caught a price-shown vs price-charged mismatch invisible in code), performance/layout audits, and security scans for leaked keys and access-control flaws. The idea worth keeping is the evidence-labelling discipline, where every agent finding must cite captured proof, and black-box QA of a running app with no code access as a review-loop step.

title: 6 Insane Trending GitHub AI Design Repos You Need to Use
summary: A roundup of six GitHub repos that give coding agents better design inputs: an Awards MCP for studying real award-winning sites, Responsively for multi-viewport screenshot checks, Genjutsu skills (including Bunshin, a sub-agent build-and-review loop), Dem Brand for extracting a site's styles into design.md, App Store Screenshots, and Brag for launch videos. The idea worth keeping is Bunshin's pattern: a lead agent sets a shared style, sub-agents build pages in parallel, and reviewer agents send problems back for fixes. The rounds stop at a round limit, when only minor issues remain, or when a round fixes nothing, though results varied by style.

title: Vercel's CEO Just Unveiled The Greatest AI Coding Workflow Ever
summary: Vercel's CEO describes working with AI agents: test ideas in throwaway projects, track whether the work is drifting from the plan rather than how much is shipped, and use adversarial agents to stress-test, scan for security debt and act on customer feedback fast. The video (AI Labs) turns this into seven tips, with commands and agents like a direction-drift checker, a breaker agent, and a first-time-user agent restricted by a hook to only running the app. The idea worth keeping is a drift check that compares what agents built against the PRD/spec folder, since building is cheap and agents never push back on scope.

title: Build Your Own AI Software Factory with Claude Code
summary: Builds a software factory inside an existing repo from one prompt: a /factory skill as orchestrator, seven sub-agents (spec writer, builder, four parallel reviewers, approver) and markdown files as the only state. Jobs loop through review at most three rounds, the approver escalates money, deploy and product calls to a human, and git worktrees let several jobs run at once.

title: EGM: Google's New Way To Use Claude Code Is Insane
summary: Google's Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) is a spec-driven workflow where a context-rich main agent (the elephant) brainstorms and drafts a design doc with the user. Context-free sub-agents (the goldfish) then review it from several angles, such as simpler alternatives, scale issues, and whether the spec is clear enough to build from. The idea worth keeping is that reviewers should never see the planning chat, so they can't just agree with the planner. The workflow also has a drift report that compares per-folder READMEs against the code.

title: This Is Microsoft's New Plan To Fix Claude's Usage Limits
summary: Microsoft's Token Economizer is a Claude Code/Codex plugin that learns from your past sessions to cut token use: it records repeated mistakes as 'micro skills', disables tools unused across sessions, and nudges the agent when it gets stuck. Microsoft reports 23-31% lower cost on 277 bugs with no loss in fixes, though it costs more at first and only pays off after about six tasks per project. The idea worth keeping is to treat wasted tokens as a feedback loop: mine session history for repeated failures and unused tool definitions, then feed them back as project facts and pruned tool sets.

title: Anthropic Just Released A New System For Using Claude Code
summary: Anthropic's Claude Code team claims that as agents write far more code, the bottleneck is review, so they front-load verification with evals, use a separate reviewer agent, and tier checks by risk. The video turns this into a workflow of skills: write-eval, a builder/verifier/reviewer loop with fresh-context subagents, a review.md of learned rules, a risk classifier, a first-time-user agent, and a git-based fix-a-bug skill. The idea worth keeping is to cap builder/reviewer loops (rethink after 3 rounds, review only the latest diff, name the problem class), since about 59% of reviewer findings were repeats.

title: Deepseek Just Released The Greatest Claude Code Workflow Ever
summary: DeepSeek's 'super agent' splits work between a router session that only talks to you and dispatches tickets, and worker agents that each build one ticket in their own context window and worktree. In their test of five runs each, the slowest task took 15.7 min versus 29.5 min for a single session using sub-agents, because the single session kept doing the work itself and was interrupted by new messages. The idea worth keeping is to separate talking to the human from doing the work, and to feed the router self-contained tickets (a requirements file plus an eval file) so workers never need to ask questions, with the router checking results against the eval.

title: Head Of Design At X's New Claude Skill Is Insane
summary: Benji Taylor (head of design at X) packaged his landing-page demo design process as a skill called Stage Show, claiming agents fail at animated product demos because they lack taste and draw generic fake UIs. The skill walks the agent through seven steps (placement, look, story, start from one of ~40 real examples, fill screen, motion, self-check) and closes with a verification loop that records the running demo, lays the frames out on one contact sheet, and uses a small program to flag overflow and jumps. The idea worth keeping: make the agent verify motion by recording it and checking frames programmatically, and gate handoff on that check passing, instead of reading code or taking a single static screenshot.

title: This Finally Cut Claude Code's Token Usage In Half
summary: The video claims Claude Code's built-in web tool wastes tokens on page markup and menus, and that it only reads the first 13% of a long page verbatim while a smaller model summarizes the next 34% and the last 53% goes unread. An open-source CLI called OC (onlycli) instead returns a ~500-token numbered outline that the agent navigates section by section, saving about 21% of tokens on a single task and about 20% (3.9M vs 4.9M) on a five-agent research run. The idea worth keeping is to give agents a cheap outline and let them pull in only the sections they need, instead of loading whole pages into context.

title: Creator Of The Best Design Skill Just Unveiled His AI Design Workflow
summary: Leon Lin, author of the trending Taste Skill, argues that good AI-generated design comes from a structured process rather than prompt wording: short prompts with 9-12 visual references, a mockup as a target, a numeric quality bar, long time budgets, banned-pattern lists, design-then-animation staging, specific feedback, and independent judges. His 'cook' skill packages this as a loop of build, screenshot, compare to references, and review by fresh-context judges (possibly a different model) until a score threshold such as 9.2/10 is met. The idea worth keeping: don't let the builder agent grade its own work. Use separate-context, cross-model judges plus a numeric bar, and tell the agent its self-score is inflated.

title: Fable 5.2 Is Insane... Only If You Use It Anthropic's Way
summary: The video distills nine rules from Anthropic's Claude Code team (Lydia Hallie, Addy Osmani) and launch guidance for using Fable 5.2: start on Opus 5.5 and escalate only when needed, define verifiable finish lines up front, and use Fable as the lead agent that delegates to cheaper Sonnet, Opus and Haiku workers. It also covers running the lead on high effort, pre-authorizing safe steps so long runs don't stall, writing final reports for readers who never watched the work, trimming old 'never/important' lines from CLAUDE.md, and compacting before model switches to avoid cache loss. The idea worth keeping is the split of roles: a strong model plans and reviews in a fresh session against pass/fail checks, while cheaper models build. Sub-agent cost notes in CLAUDE.md cut spawning by about half, and the setup only pays off on big jobs.

title: Google Just Released Something To Fix Claude Code's Biggest Problem
summary: Google measured agent distraction across millions of internal sessions and found that agents chase stale or unrequested 'side quests' (e.g. old TODO notes tied to already-fixed bugs), which cost 70% more actions, 77% more tokens and over twice the time. Outdated CLAUDE.md files, specs and memory notes cause the same drift, with agents following the stale file about 9 times in 10. The idea worth keeping: treat the code as the source of truth, tag tickets with status, and run a periodic sweep that verifies a note is stale against history (via an independent checker agent) before archiving it.

title: NVIDIA Just Released Something To Fix Claude Skills
summary: NVIDIA's open-source Skill Evaluator audits agent skills in three tiers: a deterministic, no-LLM lint of structure, security and description truncation, then LLM-based duplicate-instruction detection, then A/B task runs with and without the skill in a sandbox. The video claims agent-written skills drift from best practice over iterative edits, with long descriptions cut off at the character limit so the 'when to use' text never reaches the model. The idea worth keeping is to score a skill by running the same task with and without it, and to treat scanner findings as triage, since many security flags were false alarms.
